maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SPEAKER OF UNITED KINGDOM HOUSE

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SPEAKER OF UNITED KINGDOM HOUSE
speechtext:
I wish to draw the attention of hon. members to the presence in the gallery of Right Hon. Horace King, Speaker of the British House of Commons. It is indeed a privilege to welcome Mr. Speaker King to the Canadian House of Commons, a house inspired by the same traditions and concepts as the ancient and honourable chamber over which he presides.
We in Canada have welcomed many distinguished guests during this our centennial year. Some have been heads of state, others have been heads or members of governments. But Mr. King's sphere of jurisdiction is strictly parliamentary and he thus calls forth from us, the members of the Canadian House of Commons, a very special greeting.
We Canadian parliamentarians are aware that the concepts of liberty we cherish are nowhere more fittingly embodied than in the person of the Speaker who presides over the most historic legislative assembly in the commonwealth. Seven hundred years of parliamentary evolution have transformed the Speaker's position from that of an obscure spokesman with somewhat unenviable and uncertain duties to one of the most honoured and respected public offices in the realm. Doctor King occupies an office which can be traced almost without a break back to the fourteenth century, even to the remote origins of the institution of parliament.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)

True to a long parliamentary tradition, Mr. Speaker King has to his credit an honourable record of service which brought new lustre to the Chair of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom. His visit to Ottawa, the first by a British Speaker to the parliament of Canada is a joy and an honour.
Mr. Speaker, you are welcome among your colleagues and your friends of the Canadian House of Commons.

We are extremely pleased and honoured to welcome you, Mr. Speaker, in your personal
capacity and for the great parliamentary ideal which you represent.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SPEAKER OF UNITED KINGDOM HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ENFORCEMENT AND IMPROVEMENT OF TRAFFIC CONTROL PROCEDURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. In view of the near tragedy at Malton airport last Monday, involving an Air Canada DC-8 and a small private plane, and in view of other similar occurrences in recent months, will the minister take appropriate measures to ensure that air traffic control procedures and other safety measures are strictly enforced and, if necessary, improved?

subtopic: ENFORCEMENT AND IMPROVEMENT OF TRAFFIC CONTROL PROCEDURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a general question which it is difficult to deal with on orders of the day, but certainly I appreciate the problem. Of course the answer to the question is that the department makes every effort to enforce its regulations in order to guarantee the safety of Canadian air passengers. However, that is becoming increasingly difficult, as my hon. friend will appreciate, with the volume of traffic increasing at a tremendous rate and the number of light planes now being operated by Canadian individuals.
This puts an extra demand on the department to provide additional facilities, and the department is studying on a national basis

what it can do in the years ahead to move some of the light plane traffic away from the international airports in order to make it easier for them and facilitate long range travel.

subtopic: REQUEST OF BAR ASSOCIATION FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I begin I should like to say that the fact that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) last night in the budget debate touched upon the question of foreign affairs was of great interest to me and, I am sure, to the rest of the house. Normally this is not done in a budget debate, but I think it was timely and important that he did so because it is my belief, which may be surprising to most of us in this house, that foreign affairs is the subject which concerns Canadians most at the present time.
Although I do not intend to devote much of my speech this morning to this subject, let me simply say in summary that it is my impression that people all over Canada want, in a bi-partisan sense, more clarity and more Canadian content in our foreign affairs posture. They do not want differences for differences sake. They understand only too well that an independent foreign policy is difficult for a nation such as Canada in 1967. Without being anti-American, Canadians are worried that too much of our foreign affairs policy is dictated by Washington. I do not think this is necessarily the case. It is easier to discuss it than to act.
I think more Canadians would like to see Canada play a greater peace making rather than a peace keeping role. While we must honour many of our traditional commitments such as NORAD and NATO, Canada should display-and I think Washington would welcome this-more initiative and experimentation in this field, something that is not now provided to Washington with its world leadership role in the field of foreign affairs. In view of the fact that perhaps the real challenge is one of an economic nature in areas such as Latin America, Asia, Africa and southeast Asia, this realignment of our foreign affairs posture will certainly affect our budgetary expenses. Therefore I think it was timely that the President of the Privy Council should have brought up this subject last night.
Let me give my opinion on the following subject in brief summary. I have no scientific backing for it, but it is my belief that the things that are concerning Canadians most today, in order of importance, are first, foreign affairs; second, on the domestic scene, taxes and the cost of living, and that is what I intend to speak about this morning; third, national unity; and fourth, political leadership, not only relating to the quality of in-
[Mr. Speaker.)

dividual leaders but relating to the capacity of our institutions, both federal and provincial, to solve the kind of problems that are facing a modern state and its provinces.
As I said, sir, the second most important issue that is concerning Canadians today is taxes and the rising cost of living. The sounding we conducted-and I admit it was not a scientific sounding, of which there are plenty today, but a political one, although not political in the narrow sense of the word-gave us an indication of what the Canadian people were thinking in relation to taxes and the cost of living.
In summary this is what we found. Tremendous concern is shown for the amount of money it is taking people to live these days. Although complaints about taxes have existed as long as taxes themselves, the problem of inflation has not. In general people want the government to exercise more restraint in spending so as to keep taxes down. They want people living on fixed incomes, especially pensioners, to be given a break, and they want the government to tackle inflation before it prices food, for example, right out of their reach. Last week we found that housing is being priced right out of the reach of the people, but I have found, after speaking to thousands of Canadians in every corner of this nation, that today food also is being priced right out of the reach of the people. So Canadians at the grass roots level, no matter what the minister says, expect the federal government to start tackling the problem of inflation and the rising cost of living.
Let us look at the background of this whole problem. Let us go back nine, ten or eleven years. Like the President of the Privy Council I do not want to be inadvertently partisan, and regardless of who was in power at that time let us review in general summary our approach to the problems, of the cost of living, inflation and high prices. In those days both the elected representatives and the economic experts agreed it was a serious matter and it was not a situation with which we would necessarily have to live. Prosperity in the true and profound sense of the word did not mean that we had to get used to spiralling costs and inflation, and if we really were going to have prosperity we should at all times confront the problem of inflation and high prices. So ten years ago there was a general feeling that publicly elected officials and economists would take the problem of inflation seriously, and that it had to be met head on by the federal government.
October 6, 1967

The phrase "by the federal government" leads me to my second contention, namely that ten years ago there was absolutely no doubt about the proposition that it was the federal government which had the primary responsibility to exercise leadership and meet this problem head on. What do we find today? We find this government approaching the problem of inflation in the same way it does every other issue that faces and concerns the Canadian people; that is, by hiding behind the constitution. The Minister of Finance invokes the constitution in exactly the same way as the hon. gentleman who is now sitting beside him did last week on the housing crisis.
What this government should do is go on a national tour and wave the constitution in front of all those people who are faced with these myriad problems. The government say "We cannot do anything; the constitution says we cannot". This government cannot keep fooling the people. Every time a pressing national problem comes up the government gives a little lecture to the municipalities and a little lecture to the provinces and then says to the public "We would like to act but we cannot because of the constitution." The same government whose Prime Minister travels right across the country saying "The real problem today is that there are far too many powerful provincial premiers encroaching on the national interest and chiselling away at federal powers" invokes the constitution every time a national issue comes up such as housing, inflation, air, water and soil pollution, urban development, and highway and automobile deaths and injuries. The government say "We are not going to do anything" and then wonder why people are losing faith in federal leadership.
Lack of federal leadership is another issue about which the Canadian people in every corner of this land are talking. The government has abdicated its responsibilities in all areas involving national issues. No matter what this government says, its attitude today is that it does not consider the high cost of living, inflation and spiralling prices as serious matters. It is not doing much if anything about them, except to inform the nation from time to time that it is chipping away at expenditures here and there. This is what the Minister of Finance tells us from time to time. We wonder how successful he is going to be.
The government is projecting the idea that it is not taking the question seriously. This is the situation today as opposed to the situation ten years ago when there was no doubt about
The Budget-Mr. Grafftey
who had the responsibility in this matter. The government again invokes the constitution.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
In case I am accused of being partisan, Mr. Speaker, let me refer to some more objective sources. Let me refer to the warning given by the International Monetary Fund, something I do not believe it would do lightly. I think bodies like the International Monetary Fund are pretty careful before doing anything that might look as if they are involving themselves in the domestic concerns of nations. So I am sure it was only after much thought and hard work this summer and much, if you will, diplomatic consideration that the International Monetary Fund issued a public warning to the minister and to the government to the effect that they would have to wake up and deal with the problem of inflation if the economy of this country is going to be healthy in the true sense of the word. In addition to the International Monetary Fund the Economic Council of Canada, another independent, non-political body, similarly warned the government.
The Canadian people in every corner of the country are, generally speaking, saying one thing about this government. The picture is not all doom and gloom, though perhaps the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) will accuse me of being a little irresponsible by painting a doom and gloom picture. In spite of this government, say the people, there are many healthy signs in the economy and its future potential. But the general feeling is that as a result of its ill timed and ill considered fiscal, monetary and spending policies this government has destroyed the options open to it and in fact is mismanaging the economy.
I have attempted to pinpoint the background of the problem, Mr. Speaker, and to outline my view that while we must have the co-operation of the municipalities, of industry and of labour in meeting the problems, of inflation and the cost of living, it is the federal government which must give leadership and confront this problem, thus giving the people the feeling that the federal government is leading them in this regard.
Just in case hon. members opposite do not feel that the cost of living today is a serious problem, Mr. Speaker, let me ask them whom it affects. I sometimes think we are a little smug about this, and I have no wish to be demagogic in this regard. It is true that we are blessed with a young country which enjoys the second highest standard of living in the history of the world, but this is small
October 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Grafftey comfort to the 25 per cent to 30 per cent of the people who are ill housed and who live in deprivation, poverty, even destitution.
These conditions have been defined by, I think it is, the Ontario labour council. They define poverty as a family of four living on an income of under $3,000; destitution as a family of four living on under $2,000; and deprivation as a family of four living on under $4,000. What about the 500,000 rural families living on net annual incomes of under $2,000?
What is the government doing for our pensioners and people who live on fixed and shrinking incomes, those who are suffering from poverty amidst plenty? This hard-pressed core of our society is being affected by inflation and the cost of living.
Those of us whose salaries, investment income or other forms of income rise to compensate us for the increasing cost of living also complain a little, but we are nowhere nearly as badly off as those people living in deprivation, destitution or poverty on shrinking and fixed incomes. These are the people who are affected by inflation and the cost of living, and it does not serve us well to boast about the general high standard of living in Canada and the fact that we have the second highest economic standard of living in the world while this situation confronts us.
What does democracy mean, Mr. Speaker, to these people who are living in grinding poverty, who are faced with spiralling costs which price food out of their hands, who are confronted by a government that shoves statistics relating to housing or the cost of living in front of them and does not give them any feeling that it will grapple with the problem and take some action to correct it? The government does not take the problem seriously. It is a government that, when it is confronted with an immediate problem demanding immediate action, does one of many things. It cites the constitution and says we are going to have a federal-provincial conference on the constitution. We are told we are going to have a symposium on the problem at various points across the country. We are told that studies are going to be conducted. We are told about parliamentary joint committees and task forces.
However, Mr. Speaker, this government cannot fool the people any longer. Of course modern problems demand study and the allocation of research dollars. There are times when there is need for studies to be made, and I am not against studies. But there is also a time to act, and I must say that this is the most inactive, retrograde government that we


have ever seen in the history of this country. I ask the government not to be afraid of leadership in the area of housing or inflation. The people want the government to lead. The trouble with this government is that it has abdicated its responsibilities, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
I know my sophisticated friend in the back row does not like speeches that come from the heart, but I might tell him that if he only went to his people he would soon discover the facts. He probably thinks I am being demagogic. I realize he was automatically elected in the big swing, but if he would keep close to his people he would soon find there is want in this country. If some politicians speak passionately occasionally it is because they know the problems of their people.
The No. 2 problem with this government, Mr. Speaker, is that it is dominated in its ministry and on its front benches by those who have a bureaucratic attitude. We have a wonderful bureaucracy which is second to none, but I am sure the bureaucrats themselves are worried at the fact that the front benches of the Liberal party are dominated by ex-senior civil servants, including the Minister of Finance. I suggest this is one reason the hon. member who just interrupted me is out of touch with his own people, and why I doubt whether he will stay in office much longer.
If I am demagogic, Mr. Speaker, I do not apologize for one moment. I suggest that hon. members opposite who share the views of the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) take a trip across the country and speak to the people and they will soon discover that there is want and poverty amidst plenty in Canada today.
One reason there is inflation and a rising cost of living in this country, creating greater and greater hardship on those living in destitution, poverty and deprivation, is this. I think we often mislead ourselves in terms of what we consider to be social welfare legislation. These laws are passed admittedly by men whose hearts are in the right place, and I like to think that every member of this house has the best of intentions. But it is not good enough, Mr. Speaker, just to have your heart in the right place; you have to pass legislation that will work. And the problem with much of the universal welfare legislation we have passed in the months and years that have gone by is that it is not reaching the
October 6, 1967	COMMONS
root source of poverty among the people it is primarily designed to help.
[DOT] (12 noon)
I think of the pension plan that was passed a number of years ago in the house. In many ways it was good legislation. On numerous instances we attempted to amend it. Of course, ministers of the government and the President of the Privy Council referred to this earlier and they trotted out the old, "have you stopped beating your wife" argument. They asked, "How did you vote?" Everybody knows how we voted on medicare. Yet time and time again, both in the house and in committee, we attempted to amend that legislation.
The difficulties of those in the lower income groups and those living in grinding poverty are coumpounded because many of our classically considered welfare programs are not reaching them and do not help. The pension plan does not help many of the poorest in the rural areas. We told the government that this would happen. We voted for the bill but we tried, tried and tried again to amend the legislation so that it would help those who need help most. After all, the way welfare programs help those in need is the criterion by which they are judged. One does not ask, "How did you vote?"
I say, therefore, that because of the confusion in relations between Ottawa and the provinces and because our normal social welfare legislation is not reaching the root at which it is aimed, the problem of poverty in the midst of plenty is becoming increasingly aggravated. I am fully aware that the grass roots will say: We want our taxes to be reduced and our social welfare benefits to be increased. Such an attitude puts many politicians on both sides of the house on the spot occasionally. No one can have his cake and eat it.
Years ago I felt that many reactionary politicians had the attitude that any initiative by the public sector was retrograde. Let us be frank with ourselves and the people. In this young country we shall have to build many more hospitals, universities, schools and roads. We shall need a great deal of expenditure in the public sector. We realize now that the private sector moves forward only when the public sector has done its part. This modern approach to government and political attitudes makes it more important than ever for us to plan our economic and social spending priorities in Ottawa and with the provinces.

What do we mean by planning our spending priorities? This was alluded to last night. Many in this house espouse varying shades of political philosophy. The job will be difficult, but we were elected to face difficulties. Ordering our spending priorities is difficult, but we must do so. We all know the problems that face all levels of modern government. The sooner the federal government convenes the proper kind of meeting with the provinces, in fact, with all levels of government, and begins to plan spending priorities, the better it will be for us. Until that happens the difficulties we face will become worse.
The trouble is that we have no guarantee that the government believes in the necessity to co-operate with the provinces in terms of organizing and ordering social and economic spending priorities. This will not be easy. This government has always felt that it has a mandate from heaven to tell the people what is best for them. You cannot force your opinion down people's throats today. Modern communications make it important for us to see that there is municipal, provincial and federal co-operation so that our system works. I say, as I have said again, again and again, that while the task will not be easy the government must open that kind of dialogue with provincial elected representatives and officials which will show our people that there is planning and order in our spending priorities.
As I said before, every hon. member probably has his heart in the right place. Nevertheless, we have only so much money. I am sure that the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) would like to print more, but there is only so much to go around. This is becoming increasingly apparent. Expenditures are growing and growing but we can only do so much at one time. The people want an end to the continuing conflict and air of tension between levels of government. People all over Canada are sick and tired that no level of government is confronting seriously many of the modern problems facing the nation. Everywhere in Canada people are talking about the cost of living, housing, air pollution, soil and water pollution, automobile highway deaths and injuries and many other things What is happening in this country is probably happening in no other country in the western world. There is a feeling among our people that no level of government alone, and no government acting in concert with governments at other levels, is confronting these problems.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the speech of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) which he described as a passionate address. I wish to comment on his statement that within the cabinet ranks and within the Liberal party there are so many members from what he described as the bureaucracy. He referred, of course, to those who, having retired from brilliant careers in the Canadian civil service, have entered the public life of Canada by being elected and entering this house. It is curious indeed that after five years in office my hon. friend's party did not make itself attractive to anybody in the bureaucracy, as he describes it. How many of these people went to sit on my hon. friend's side of the house? I should think that if anybody in Canada were able to judge political parties it would be those who had so ably served them. It certainly must be a judgment in itself that none of them has seen fit to seek office and sit on that side of the house, having experienced a Conservative administration between 1957 and 1963.

We must remember when we discuss the budget today that we are discussing a budget which was brought down in the spring. The summer recess has passed and there has been plenty of time for the country, and for representatives of business and industry in particular, to reflect on matters pertaining to the budget and to finance generally. One of the subjects which has occupied the minds of those who take a serious attitude toward these questions is, of course, the massive Carter report presented in the spring. Some

hon. members have had an opportunity to digest it during the summer months, as have a number of people associated with business and industry.
One of the points which caused greatest alarm when the report was issued was a suggestion that a massive overhaul was needed in the system of taxing mines, gas and oil wells and the extractive industry generally. This suggestion resulted in so many protests that the minister gave certain assurances to the industry in the course of a statement he made in the house on May 11, 1967 when he said, as reported in Hansard at page 111:
A number of taxpayers have made representations to us that in some instances the very uncertainty introduced by the royal commission report is causing them to act as though the recommendations of the commission had been adopted by the government.
A little later he said:
We have given careful study to see what we could do at this time to minimize these uncertainties without prejudicing the government's freedom of action in determining the ultimate shape of the tax reform it will propose to parliament.
Further on in his statement the minister described two undertakings which he believed appropriate to give in order that those concerned could carry on with the development of important projects in respect of which incentive provisions now in the law were important. He said:
The first undertaking concerns the three-year exemption for new mines. We have concluded that should the government decide to propose the removal of this incentive it would not do so in a manner which would remove the exemption with respect to income earned before January 1, 1974, nor would it in any essential manner change the method of application of that exemption before that date.
He went on to say:
The second undertaking concerns the treatment presently accorded to prospectors and their backers under section 83 of the Income Tax Act. Should the government decide to impose the withdrawal of this incentive, we would not do so with respect to amounts received before January 1, 1969 that relate to properties or interests acquired before January 1, 1968.
These assurances were welcome, but they are relatively short-term assurances giving an indication to the mining industry that a complete overhaul of the tax system will not in any event take place in the course of the next few years.

The Brenda payroll will reach $3.0 million annually, with employment of 350.

In conclusion I should like to say that industry in Canada cannot live and expand unless it exists in a long-term climate of confidence. It must receive that if investment is to flow into Canadian industry. I say this is particularly so in respect of the mining and extractive industries of Canada because it takes an enormous amount of exploration in order to find a mine. Once a mine has been found a great deal of work must be done in order to bring it up to the production stage. Even many of those which turn out to be producers are not the most successful producers. When we analyse the situation we find that 3,000 claims have to be discovered in order to produce one good mine. It is for these reasons that incentives must exist if this great industry is to flourish in Canada.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I should like to make these few points. There must be long-term assurances that the mining industry is not going to be upset by massive changes in the methods of providing incentives and imposing taxes. There must be long-term assurances that investment from abroad will be welcomed in Canada. There


must be long-term assurances that the total sum of taxes levied on industry is not going to creep up to the point where taxes are greater than the total levy of taxes which allows the possibility for Canadian dollars to compete with United States dollars, for example. We must be able to give the assurance to industry in Canada that we can settle the question of confederation and do so quickly so that foreign capital can move into Canada with these investors being able to be confident of a stable economic climate.
Anyone who read the stories which appeared this morning in the business section of the Globe and Mail, or listened to what Mr. Kierans said recently in Quebec, must be aware of what I have in mind. It is in respect of these points that the mining industry must have long-term assurances in order that it may continue to exist and flourish. Thank you, sir, for your kindness.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) on the excellent speech he has just delivered. It is regrettable that its general tone and tenor should be so out of tune with what we hear from the front benches of his party and that he along with other members of his party from British Columbia who occupy the back benches should be listened to so little by their own ministers who have the responsibility for the decisions which are made concerning our province. Let me remind the hon. member, who I am sure feels that there is very little attention given him over there, that he would be welcome at any time to join us here in raising his voice on behalf of British Columbia.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I just want to say to the hon. member that I can raise my voice from this position very well and frequently do so.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is exactly what I am saying. The hon. member raises his voice very well but it has very little effect. That is the problem.
This morning I should like to refer to an article by Alex Young which appeared in the Vancouver Province on Monday, October 2. It appeared in the column "Victoria Comment" under the heading "Other Provinces More Equal Than B.C.", and it points out some of the problems to which the previous speaker alluded and which are very real to the province of British Columbia. The article was
October 6, 1967

based on some comments by the hon. Kenneth Kiernan, minister of recreation and conservation in the Social Credit government of British Columbia.
He is concerned, as are a great many British Columbians, about the consistent failure of the federal government to carry out policies that would be equitable across Canada. He gives various examples as cited in this article. One has to do with the question of purchases by British Columbia from the central provinces and sales from British Columbia to the central provinces. Of course there is no obvious barrier in this regard because there are no interprovincial tariffs, but he does point out the effect that the present tariff policy has on the province.
It is pointed out in this article that British Columbia buys from the rest of Canada some three to five times as much goods in dollar value as it sells. The goods sold to the rest of Canada are to a large extent sold at world prices but the goods bought from the rest of Canada by British Columbia to a large extent carry a substantial tariff protection mark-up over world prices. The tariff protection markup on British Columbia goods sold to the central provinces is perhaps $10 million over world prices on a year's business. On the other hand, the tariff protection on goods bought from the central provinces is estimated at a tariff mark-up of over $100 million a year over world prices. The people of British Columbia pay that mark-up.
Mr. Kiernan is also concerned about aid by Canada as a whole in respect of local projects and the fact that British Columbia cannot obtain direct federal grants for such things as the Peace River or Columbia River projects or the Pacific Great Eastern Railway development. Yet the central government can put up huge amounts for the Saskatchewan dam, the St. Lawrence seaway or the projected Northumberland Strait causeway. He believes that national policies should have national application on an equitable basis.
This whole question and its reference to this budget debate was emphasized by the reply the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) made on October 4 to a question raised in the house in respect of exports of Japanese fiber to Canada. At that time the minister said, as recorded at page 2800 of Hansard for that date:
Mr. Speaker, the government has already invited the Japanese government to do that.
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
He was referring to a restriction on these exportations of fiber to Canada. The Minister of Finance went on to say:
When I was in Rio I had the opportunity of speaking directly to the Japanese minister of finance in order to support our application.
I do not know whether the minister when he was in Rio was aware that there had been a debate in this house at about the same time on the question of the disappearing market for Canadian wheat in Japan. However, if the Japanese minister of finance had been aware of the debate which took place in this house I am sure he would have been most perplexed at the request of the Minister of Finance.
I was very surprised the other day, when the Minister of Finance made this remarkable statement, that no member in this house representing the grain-growing regions of the prairie provinces got to his feet to ask a supplementary question. I suspect they missed the significance of the reply in relation to this major industry on the prairies. I hope that was the case and that they have not in the last few weeks turned their eyes to the Atlantic area so much that they feel their policy has changed to the extent they can make no objection.
In this regard I again should like to compliment the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford) for his promptness in asking a supplementary question at that time and point out that although he speaks very ably on behalf of his province, as did the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, his words seem to fall on ears that are strangely deaf. We do have a set of tariff policies and it seems to be the government's intention, if we can accept the words of the Minister of Finance, to carry out actively a policy that has long-range discriminatory effects against exports from British Columbia and from the west, continuing a trend that is becoming increasingly important to us.
9 (12:50 p.m.)
The gap between our sales to Japan and our imports from Japan has been constantly growing. It is increasing annually. Usually we in the west attribute to the east the quality of inscrutability. But one fails to understand the government's actions in this regard, having listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) defending the position of his government during the wheat debate and saying that a most aggressive sales drive is in progress and then having heard the Minister of Finance a couple of days later confessing that the drive is not all that aggressive. One wonders what his reaction would be if the
2888	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Johnston Japanese government requested the Canadian government to restrict our wheat sales to Japan.
This matter is all the more important when we realize that the results of the Kennedy round, which have been hailed so much in this debate and over the last few months, are being severely threatened at the moment by a massive onslaught by protectionist interests in the United States. We cannot assume that the objectives of the Kennedy round of negotiations have been accomplished. Just the other day the house of representatives passed a bill which could have a most damaging effect on the whole concept of tariff reductions resulting from the Kennedy round. We hope that the government gives the matter of trade with Japan and in fact with the entire Pacific rim the importance which it claims it does. After all, this is the government whose Prime Minister went to British Columbia just a few months ago and told that province not to go out on its own into the Pacific rim in order to extend trade, that the federal government will look after the interests of the west in that area. He said it very clearly. Yet I am sure, after the approach of the Minister of Finance to the Japanese minister of finance in Rio the other day, it will take all the charm, ability and good will of the whole cabinet and of the premier of British Columbia in order to undo the damage that was done. British Columbia will have to go forth, independently of any decision made in Ottawa in order to sell its products and extend its trade in the Pacific rim.
I was also very interested in the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis). This summer he made an extensive tour of the province of British Columbia together with a great many parliamentary secretaries and cabinet ministers. I do not quite know the reason for all this activity. One would hope it was in the best interests of British Columbia, but I suspect that the motivation lay elsewhere. I can assure the house that the trails through the province were well worn by these representatives of the government who should be able now to come back to this house and speak clearly and ably on behalf of that part of Canada. However, I am afraid this was not the reason nor the purpose of their visit.
The Minister of Finance was among those who made that pilgrimage. I regret I was not in the town of Salmon Arm when he invited himself to the Liberal conference there and spoke with the good people of the interior of British Columbia. I hope he paid careful at-

DEBATES	October 6, 1987
tention to what they had to tell him about the trade situation and about the development which the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra outlined in his speech.
The hon. member for Coast-Capilano said some interesting things about the designated area program when he was in the Okanagan valley. The Okanagan area seemed to be a very popular place with many of the ministers and parliamentary secretaries who visited it. I know that the scenic beauty and the climate which prevailed during this most beautiful summer would attract almost anyone but I doubt that it was the lakes, the air and the skies that caused this sudden interest.
The hon. member spoke about the possibility of ending the designated area program in the Okanagan valley in the near future. I would be the first one to say that this program has been of great benefit to the area but I feel that the benefits it has brought to British Columbia and to the Okanagan valley are in a sense just beginning and that if that area is redesignated it would leave for practical purposes no part of the province of British Columbia within the designated area. The only part of British Columbia left in the designated area would be the town of Fernie which has not yet succeeded in attracting any significant industry despite the program. At the same time, throughout the rest of Canada there are still very extensive areas involved in this program.
We know that the Department of Industry saw fit to remove the Skookumchuk area of east Kootenay from the designated area program when it became apparent that a very important pulp and paper mill would be constructed there. So the benefits of this program to the province have not been very great considering the total sum in grants paid out. They do not compare with what has been spent in Ontario, Quebec or almost any other province one could name. An early end to the program in British Columbia would be one more example of an inequitable national policy on the part of this government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had been talking about the policies of the government in relation to the province of British Columbia and had referred in particular to a recent speech by the hon. member for
October 6, 1967	COMMONS
Coast-Capilano while he was in the Okanagan region in which he made reference to the designated area grants. Yesterday he also made reference to the development of the coal deposits in the southeastern corner of the province in the Fernie area and stated quite bluntly that he was opposed to government subsidies for the development of this resource.
What he did not do at the same time was to indicate his position on the extension of the Great Northern Railway to Fernie, which is certainly a most important issue. If there is no subsidy and the Canadian Pacific Railway is not going to haul this coal there is still one alternative left in that area, but the hon. member failed to make it at all clear where he stood on that matter.
When the hon. member for Coast-Capilano speaks he speaks from a little different position than the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra or the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard inasmuch as we do not know whether he is speaking with an official voice. We do know that sitting on that side of the house he has hopes and aspirations. What we do not know is whether he is merely flying a kite or telling us what is the policy of the federal government. I hope that we will have greater clarification from the hon. member on some of these points.
This then, Mr. Speaker, is the main burden of my remarks. I have tried to illustrate the concern that we in the west have that policies will be favourable to us. We knew, as I am sure the Minister of Finance knew when he spoke to the Japanese representative about textiles, that these textiles were not being dumped in Canada but were coming into this country through the ordinary process of trade. We have that on the authority of Mr. Grey, the assistant deputy minister of finance, and the minister himself must surely have been aware of that. Although he advocates free trade, we in the west should like some indication that this is what the policy of the federal government is intended to promote.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote not Mr. Kiernan, a cabinet minister in the British Columbia government, but rather the writer of an article which appeared in the Province for Monday, October 2 last. After listing certain complaints he went on to state:
These are serious complaints. Yet the reaction of federal authorities to them has tended to be more lighthearted than serious.
Perhaps there is some fun to be had in joking about affluent B.C.'s separatist tendencies. But surely it is not too much to ask that, once the

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) must have a great feeling of dread when he surveys the fiscal wreckage which surrounds him. Obviously the situation is completely out of control. Indeed, as I listened to the minister last Wednesday on television and in the house, I thought he provided a sorry spectacle. To a degree we have sympathy for him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member is very cheerful.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister has nothing to be cheerful about. He is surrounded by a mess, by a situation to which his colleagues in the cabinet have contributed. He had to make a statement in an attempt to explain the unexplainable. Perhaps he is trying to unscrew the inscrutable. He almost succeeded. Nevertheless, the unpalatable fact is that the minister has no options left to him. If he is to pay for the programs of his colleagues that call for uncontrolled spending while fighting a deficit of approximately $1 billion, he must raise taxes. If he does that he will only give his ministers more money to spend.
The minister is like a passenger in a runaway hearse and is rapidly proceeding to the edge of the precipice in the economic affairs of the country. He knows this and is concerned. I am concerned for him, because his colleagues seem so unconcerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thank the hon. member.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In Hamilton last night the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) made a speech about medicare. He was not concerned. What the Minister of Finance said last Wednesday in the house and what he said on television differs somewhat from his former speeches. I so well remember the occasion one or two years ago when he criticized the former government in words such as these which appeared in the North Hill News of Calgary on June 7, 1962:
Canada's economy was further shaken, he said, by the increasing budgetary deficits, the last one, at $475 million, "ill-timed and excessive".
The minister thought that was terrible. On another occasion this statement appeared in the Brandon Sun of June 2, 1962:
"I'm in politics," said the red-haired Mr. Sharp, "because I feel our affairs are being poorly managed. I can think of easier ways of making a living than politics, and I'm not violently partisan."
The minister is also reported to have said on that occasion, "Lester Pearson isn't a financial expert."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will buy that, Mr. Speaker. On another occasion we find the following in the Winnipeg Free Press, which is not known as being overly friendly to those on this side of the house. The date is June 2, 1962, and the headline is, "Sharp Attacks Budget Deficit". In the body of the article this appears:
The first responsibility of a Liberal government would be to restore "order to the nation's finances."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which we did.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister says "Which we did". If he calls this country's finances orderly now then I think the members of the press, the editorial writers and those who wrote the comments I have read as well as those who wrote the fourth report of the Economic Council have holes in their heads. I do not believe that is so and I do not believe the minister is correct. The situation is out of order and out of control.
We all remember the minister saying, "Our first responsibility will be to balance the budget." With that usual lack of partisan feeling which the minister is fond of displaying, he and his colleagues were condemnatory in the extreme of the former government for its deficit. Yet we face the largest deficit in the country's history. I have not compared this budget with a wartime budget but I am prone to say that this is the largest budget in our country's history, in war or peace. The minister went on to say as found in the Winnipeg Free Press of June 2, 1962:
Mr. Pearson won't be a one-man show. He listens to his advisors.
I said I was sorry for the minister's position. I only wish that his cabinet colleagues would listen to his advice. Perhaps he might get together with the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
After raising these spectres with respect to deficit financing and after saying that the government which preceded this one had been spending money like drunken sailors, the minister went on to make all sorts of promises including $2 wheat. An editorial in the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 1, 1962, describes the minister as "The Duke of Eglinton". That reminded me of another duke, the Duke of York. That duke, of course, was connected with the horse guards and hon. members may remember the saying: The grand old Duke of York, he had 10,000 men, he marched them up a very high hill and he marched them down again. When they were up they were up, when they were down they were down, but when they were only half up they were neither up nor down.

Oh, boy.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In him we had a man with some fortitude who could say no. The present minister has demonstrated that he lacks this fortitude. That is what is happening here. The minister marches his legions forth with cries of restraints to his cabinet colleagues. Then having admonished them with raised finger, he backs down again. This is evident from the conduct of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) last night. The hon. gentleman charged in the Windsor Star that the former government had "ignored the experts". How these chickens are coming home to roost. "A Balanced Budget, Sharp Pleads" says a headline in the Star. What has happened to this brave new world that the Minister of Finance envisaged? speechtext:
The minister's remedy is, of course, higher taxes. His statement the other night on television was simply an admission of this fact. It was sad viewing indeed to see the minister make this abject admission of defeat, his leadership hopes shattered. He was a picture of defeat. It was the most abject admission of failure ever made by a Canadian minister of finance. Four months ago he brought in a budget which was to have been a cure for inflation, a budget whose object was to control inflation. He expressed confidence at that time that his budgetary plan would provide all the answers. Now, four months later, he admits, as he did last Wednesday, that inflation is the single most serious problem facing Canadians.
Why is inflation so serious? It is serious because it means higher taxes, higher prices, higher rent and higher costs for business and industry. The hon. gentleman has failed completely to control inflation and he admits it. He cannot control inflation because he cannot control his colleagues. I picture him as being a mouse in a den of lions.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Some mouse.

Indeed, in order to control his spending colleagues he would have to be a fiscal Clyde Beatty and I doubt that he possesses that kind of skill. He is a member of a cabinet which should be restrained. His colleagues should be cribbed, cabined and confined. Never, since the Klondike gold rush, which occurred in the Yukon, not in Edmonton, has there been such an agglomeration of big spenders. This year they spent $11 billion. The minister's own department-and this will be difficult for him to explain-is spending $250 million more than it did last year. The hon. gentleman rushes about like a modern-day Peter the Hermit pleading for restraint. The greatest lack of restraint is shown by his own colleagues and the worst offender is the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
The Prime Minister is the author of the war on poverty, while in my own riding there are people who still live all the year round in tents. The Prime Minister, the last of the big spenders, is also the author of the war on rural poverty, a program so effective that 15,000 farmers were battering down the doors of this house to show their appreciation. Take the Company of Young Canadians. What are they doing? How much is it costing the country? Think for a moment of the $40 million art centre. It was originally to have cost around $18 million. By the time the excavations were completed the bill was already over $25 million, one of the most expensive holes in history.
One would be tempted to feel sorry for the minister if it were not for the fiscal wreckage he has created, surrounded by spendthrifts like the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Defence (Mr. Ca-dieux), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand). One can only conclude that the Minister of Finance is in complete awe of his cabinet colleagues. Reading a list of departmental spending increases in the latest estimates is like reading a litany of irresponsibility. He is being dragged along in the wake of the most spendthrift government in our history like a cork on a wave.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
He says, "Wait until you see next year's estimates. We have already cut $600 million from them." But he knows full well that this is a routine procedure that goes on year after year. It is a great joke. He tries to convince us and, worse, he tries to convince the people

of Canada that he and his government are determined to save us by cutting estimates which we have not even seen yet. This is like a car dealer who allows you a large amount on your old car on a trade-in and then adds it to the price of a new car. The saving is completely illusory.
The minister is a helpless victim of his colleague's spendthrift proclivities. Mr. Ilsley would have cracked down on this, Mr. Abbott would have stopped it, and the former member for Eglinton would have stopped it. Even the minister's predecessor in office would have stopped it, but now the situation is obviously out of control. I do not think the minister has ever been the same since he was forced to bow down to the Rockefellers. speechtext:
I think the minister cannot divest himself of the deputy minister mentality. Someone else on this side has mentioned that we are confronted with a cabinet consisting mainly of bureaucrats. I think that is the minister's whole trouble. He bows down to his cabinet colleagues. He cannot say yes or no, and so he is carried along and finds himself in a position which it is impossible for
October 6, 1967	COMMONS
him to get out of unless he raises taxes, or borrows money which he knows he cannot borrow at reasonable rates, or causes unemployment. As the minister himself described it last Wednesday, and I quote from page 2809 of Hansard:
I feel that we must-and we will-find some way to bring this inflationary movement under control even, if necessary, by letting the economy develop a little more slack for a year or two while price and cost increases taper off.
What he is advocating there is no more and no less than more unemployment. He says this will cool off the economy, but we on this side do not go for that. We see no reason why the situation cannot be controlled and at the same time keep employment opportunities as high or higher than they are now for the working force of this country.
The reports of the Auditor General in the past two or three years reveal a shocking condition of waste and extravagance. The government has utterly failed to exercise even a reasonable control over expenditures. In his 1966 report the Auditor General states that the house committee on public accounts met only once during 1965 and it did not consider the Auditor General's 1964 report. This is not to criticize the committee. It is an indication that if there is to be any control over waste something more is required.
In his latest report the Auditor General states that 49 recommendations by the public accounts committee designed to eliminate waste have not been implemented by the government. One of his recommendations concerns the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which apparently has become a byword for uncontrolled expenditure. It is all very well for the minister to rise in his place and say, "We have got to cut things to the bone." Where is the bone in the C.B.C.? There is so much fat surrounding the bone that you cannot even see it to cut it. There is to be $30 million more for the C.B.C. this year. This body, spending over $100 million a year of the taxpayers' money, apparently is completely removed from the financial control of parliament and wants to be even farther removed.
The standing committee on public accounts, a committee of this house, has on several occasions asked that the C.B.C. present written replies to the recommendations of the Glassco commission regarding the reorganization of the C.B.C. These replies have not been forthcoming. Instead the former president of the C.B.C. said at that time, "We have got our own Glassco commission." This

Perhaps these are worth-while objectives, but what control is there over these expenditures? Where is the money going and where are the explanations in this regard? These are expenditures which cannot be watched satisfactorily and there is no indication that they are being watched. Meanwhile these huge expenditures contribute to the ever-rising cost of living and the ever-rising tax rate.
This government's record is one of acting on behalf of large financial interests at the expense of ordinary Canadians. The minister asked for elaboration a moment ago. Let me elaborate in this regard. The committee on election expenses referred to these corporations which are seemingly the beneficiaries of these new programs of the Department of Industry as "friendly corporations". No wonder this government is spending more than any government in Canada's peacetime history.
The United States is fighting a war but Canada has no war. Yet our cost of living

and our taxes have risen higher than in the case of the United States. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me, I shall first open a parenthesis to explain our attitude these last few days in this corner of the house. We have been demanding that all members follow the standing orders and speak no longer than the allotted time.
We understand that the government does not want to appear to gag the members and so did not insist so far. We also understand that the official opposition being so generous towards the government has also refrained. But we have observed that some members have abused the additional time we allow them and we have seen some speaking five, ten, or even fifteen minutes more than provided for in the standing orders, while others are deprived of their right to speak.
So it is our intention in this comer of the house-and I believe that members of the Ralliement Creditistes are of my opinion-to
The Budget-Mr. Mongrain demand henceforth strict observance of the rules. We shall give at the most a couple of minutes to someone who has not finished his sentence or his speech.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I invite the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) to sit back and relax, because I shall not continue that cruel flagellation inflicted upon him for some time, as was the case for his colleague during the debate on the housing crisis. With my remarks, I shall even soothe his wounds with a little balm, and comfort him a little. To start with, however, I shall tell the house about an experiment which I carried out in my riding, which I recommend to all hon. members.
A few months ago, I sent to the 23,330 families in my new federal riding of Trois-Rivieres, among which 487 are Englishspeaking, a questionnaire made up of ten specific questions to which I requested an answer.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I think it might be interesting for the house to have an idea of what the reaction was in the riding of Trois-Rivieres. which comprises the city of Trois-Rivieres and surrounding area. The city is the second French centre in North America, since it was founded in 1634.
This is how we dealt with the questionnaire. We sent it by mail. Naturally the member paid mailing charges, and not the government. The replies were sorted out by a committee of twelve people composed of Progressive Conservatives, New Democrats, Creditistes and Independents. I am sorry to say the Liberals excused themselves as they did not want to accept, but they were replaced by a team of journalists who, to my mind, probably guaranteed as much honesty and integrity.
I am saying it for the information of hon. members, to make things quite clear, because I would not like to accuse or blame anyone and I am saying it also to reassure everyone that the hon. member did not open the mail.
Out of the 23,330 questionnaires sent out, I received 4,136 answers, approximately 17 per cent. Some questions were cancelled in some cases because they had been left unanswered.
The first question read as follows:
In your opinion, should Quebec take part In the centennial celebrations?
The replies went as follows: 3,224 people said "yes", 512 said "no" and 135 said: Decide for us, you are better informed than we are.
October 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Mongrain
The second question was as follows:
To solve the many labour conflicts are you in favour of the creation of labour courts with recognized jurisdictions?
To that question, 3,424 answered "yes", 166 answered "no", and the others did not answer.
Third question:
Should your member of parliament vote against a social measure, such as the increase of the old age pension to $105 a month, because it is supposed to be unconstitutional?
I had written "old age pension" instead of "guaranteed minimum salary" or "guaranteed minimum income". I was asking them:
Should your member of parliament vote against a social measure, in Ottawa, because it is supposed to be unconstitutional?
To this, 3,047 said "no, you should not vote against the measure", 679 said: "yes, you should vote against it".
This was the fourth question:
Do you think Quebec is ready to opt out of confederation?
Mr. Speaker, I would remind the house that Trois-Rivieres is the second largest French-speaking city and a hot-bed of separatism, since the separatist convention is to be held there at the end of the week and we have in our university and normal school, professors who mostly teach separatism.
In spite of all this, 3,300 people answered: "No, Quebec is not ready to opt out of confederation", and only 508 said:	"yes".
However, 194 said: "We do not know, please decide for us."
Of course, I am not a separatist. The decision was already made: 3,500 said "no".
Fifth question:
Are you satisfied with the general attitude of your member of parliament?
I shall give the answer with all due modesty, which, as you know, is the strong point of independent members.

I would advise the hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Choquette) to try that one in his constituency, because I would be eager to see the answer.

The sixth question was as follows:
Would It be advisable for your member to belong to a party?
Now, 2,027 electors said "no", as well as 300 or 400 other constituents, in all 2,524 who said: "No", or added: "We leave that matter to your discretion which, to me, means "no". There were 1,655 who said: "Yes, that I should belong to a party."
The seventh question read as follows:
If so, to which?
Now, 1,139 answered: "To the Liberal party" and 30 said "To the Conservative party."
Now, 104 opted for the New Democratic party, and 30 for the Creditiste party. May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the others, 2,524 in all, suggested that I remain unafRl-iated.
Item 8 was as follows:
Do you think capital punishment should be retained in some cases?
In this case, opinion is clearly just as definite, as 3,256 said "yes". I should say, Mr. Speaker, that the meaning of this question had been clearly explained on my radio program to avoid any misunderstanding. I explained that, in my estimation, to retain capital punishment in some cases means, for instance, when evidence of the murder is beyond doubt, or in cases where the crime is more sordid than others. To this, 3,256 said "yes", and only 305 said "no".
I am saying this, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it is an experience that members should try in their own constituencies. They would have what I call mathematical replies to certain rumours spread all over the country, on the question of separatism for instance.
I know that at home a very great majority of my electors are now opposed to separatism, which does not mean that they object to it, that they are not very anxious for some constitutional reforms or for up-dating the British North America Act. But, we do not go as far as the excesses the newspapers refer to concerning separatism.
Mr. Speaker, the second item I would like to deal with is that I have been listening with considerable interest to the 36 or 37 speeches that were given on housing. You have doubtless observed that I rose 23 times to ask the floor. I am probably too far away from the Chair to catch your eye. Anyway, that is past and I listen to what is being said on the budget. I come to the following conclusion.

October 6, 1967	COMMONS
It did not dawn on me to blame the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) or the present government, because I am sure after hearing all this, that the opposition could not do any better. The present government, just like the opposition, if it were in power, is operating within a capitalistic system with absolutely rigid rules which the government cannot easily evade.
So I wonder whether it is not becoming stylish to be in a state of crisis because so far, that is all we have heard about. It seems to be a standard condition to be in a state of crisis. There is the housing crisis, the labour crisis, the cost of living crisis, the constitutional crisis, the peace or war crisis if you will and tax crises. There are crises on all over.
So I wonder if the state of crisis which is becoming constant, chronic and permanent, is not recognition that the capitalist system, which we call the private enterprise system, is nearing bankruptcy.
I wonder if the greatest favour the hon. Minister of Finance could do the big shots or the big wigs, if you prefer, of our capitalist system, of private enterprise, would not be to get them together in Montmorency or elsewhere, in camera, between four walls and to tell them this: Gentlemen, it is about time that you undertake your self-criticism, your self-examination, that you ask yourselves whether the time has not come for you to suggest reforms in the old capitalist system as it has been understood for centuries, before the people grow more discontented, before they ask you for a reckoning and start a rebellion because of the way things are.
In fact, look at the strikes happening all over one after the other, look at the rebellion of the labour movements against their leaders, even against injunctions, against the law. I say that one or two demagogues a little more daring than those we already have will be enough to kindle the spark which will blow up the barrel of gunpowder. We shall wake up some day with a more or less violent revolution if our capitalistic system does not undertake its self-criticism, if it does not call for the reforms which are essential in our times.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
In 1967, people are no longer content to live as people did in 1937, 1947 and 1957 and, indeed as people did in 1867. In 1967, people want a more equitable sharing amongst the masses of the good things in life. The capitalist system, which imposes strict rules, which
DEBATES	2897
The Budget-Mr. Mongrain prevents governments from taking necessary steps, should endeavour to achieve that type of peaceful revolution which is now needed if the aspirations of the masses are to be met. Otherwise, I say it again, we will have revolutions. If the tycoons and magnates of capitalism are unwilling to indulge in self-criticism and reform, the government will be forced to propose drastic means. Otherwise, we will have far more serious and violent crises than we now have. Indeed, it will result in anarchy; the masses will revolt.
Mr. Speaker, some will think perhaps that I am raising a scare without good reason, but I ask all members of the house who are all men of good will to look into the problem dispassionately, without any regard to political partisanship-which must surely be a normal cause for concern, since the government must ward off the attack of the opposition-and to decide whether the time has not actually come for our private enterprise system to have enough sense to reform itself.
The Scriptures say, I believe, that it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God. That probably explains the obtuseness of our financial magnates and potentates who are always the last to understand the masses' demands for reform. They wait until the masses become violent. At the start, they blame the masses for their demands, their hunger, instead of asking themselves whether that hunger is not justified and should not be satisfied before the masses decide to take what they want, using whatever means are available to them, which means are not always consistent with the laws and customs of the country.
Mr. Speaker, after last week's discussion in respect of the housing crisis where we heard that this and that should be done, I think that the government should say: "Very well, so there is a housing crisis, but we cannot do any better under the circumstances". The hon. Minister of Finance has given us a brilliant explanation of the situation. The members of the opposition were saying: "This disaster came about because of the government's inefficiency". I for one do not believe in this inefficiency, and I do not think that the opposition would be more efficient. I believe that both parties are obliged to legislate within a system which does not permit, taking what I call the revolutionary measures required to fulfill today's needs.
We will not be able to curb, to hinder the demands of the masses, because, according to an old saying: "It's no use preaching to a hun-
October 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Mongrain gry man". And the Canadian people are hungry now, not only for food, for the good things that were made available by the Good Lord. When they are told that we are living in a wealthy country where the standard of living is one of the highest in the world, they say: We want our share. Whether we like it or not, we will have to give the people their share.
Mr. Speaker, I am therefore saying that the government-and I repeat it, so there will be no mistake-or the Minister of Finance would do well to convene between four walls, behind closed doors those who rule the country's finance, and invite them to do some selfexamination and take the initiative in carrying out those reforms which are necessary, instead of being content with the old traditional methods which consist of raising interest rates and increasing taxes, with the result that the little fellow always gets the worst of it. Then he demands salary increases, of course, and thus contributes to the rise of the cost of living. As a matter of fact, he never gets anywhere, once he gets a 20 per cent wage increase, the cost of living rises by 30 per cent. He is never any better off.
Mr. Speaker, I will now leave this second topic and go on right away to the third one I wanted to discuss this afternoon. I will deal very briefly with what has come to be called national unity.
An unsuccessful attempt was made the other day to start an emergency debate on that matter. The answers to my questionnaire showed that in my riding people are not separatists. But, Mr. Speaker, I think that the time has come for everyone to make his position clear in that debate and I am one of those who are sorry that the federal government lost the initiative when a provincial premier hit upon the idea, which I find brilliant, of calling the provinces together and then claimed all the credit for this idea.
I am not saying that the federal government did nothing in that respect. I know that experts are studying constitutional matters to try and satisfy the aspirations of Quebec in particular and to bring the constitution up to date to meet the needs of 1967. But that is being done too discretely. I say the federal government should publicize what it does and not allow the provinces to upstage it. After all, it is the senior government and, up to a point its attitudes are incorrectly interpreted when it is too discreet. The Canadian people then say: The federal government does not want to revise the constitution, it delays unduly a solution to that problem.


I say that, from a psychological point of view, that is bad. It gives the provinces the opportunity to take an initiative which should, to say the least, be taken simultaneously by the federal and provincial authorities, in a spirit of good will.
I continue and say this, Mr. Speaker. The rest of the country should know that the province of Quebec is no more separatist probably than the province of British Columbia, and the publicity made in that respect is exaggerated. I have given mathematical proof of that back home with the figures I quoted earlier.
I know we have our angry young men. We have our angry young men who cannot forgive their fathers and forefathers for having failed, over the last hundred years, to take advantage of all the possibilities of the Canadian constitution; who cannot forgive their fathers and forefathers for having, during the past hundred years, let themselves be led down the garden path and believe myths instead of fulfilling themselves; who also cannot forgive their English-speaking fellow-citizens for having misunderstood them so long and for not having realized the existence there of a small group with a will to live and survive. Well those young men feel frustrated and indignant; sometimes they express their wrath in a violent way. I do not approve of them for expressing it thus, through anarchy and contempt of law. However, I am ready to make allowances for those who discuss this problem and who propose extremist solutions sincerely and within the framework of the law and of our democratic system because, as I said before, they are angry young men, made furious and frustrated by the indifference of their fathers and the neglect of others, their English-speaking fellow Canadians who should have tried to understand them.
What we ask for in Quebec, Mr. Speaker, is this: equality throughout the country, not only in our own province. We do not want to be a Quebec ghetto, but full-fledged Canadians. If I were going to live in Vancouver or Winnipeg, I would want-well, if I were alone perhaps I would not ask for so much-I would want what English Canadians have in my province. In my province, English Canadians have their schools, and they are addressed in their own language at school and at the municipal and provincial levels. They are members of our clubs and of our institutions. In our courts of justice, they are addressed and are allowed to speak in their own language. They are respected; they are
October 6, 1967

treated as members of the family. There is no segregation in our province.
Well, we want French Canadians to be treated likewise throughout the country; in short, that is what we are asking.
Of course, certain expressions are currently in use: reference is made to a special status, to associate states, to a continued federalism, to complete separatism. Mr. Speaker, I am one of those who share the views expressed by the Hon. Maurice Lamontagne and published in Le Devoir on September 25 last. With your permission, I would like to quote some excerpts of his statement in order to be well understood.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
First of all, with regard to the special status, it is already in existence; this is nothing new. For 100 years, Quebec has been given special treatment, simply because our people are different from the rest of Canada, and we intend to stay different. We believe in unity through diversity.
So, Hon. Maurice Lamontagne wrote:
The idea of a special status for Quebec, as such, should not scandalize anyone. In a supplement to Le Devoir published on this subject last June 30, Mr. Jacques-Yvon Morin showed that even several Unitarian countries, while recognizing a special status for some areas, still continued to survive and develop. Also, in this supplement, Reverend Father Fdehard Ares recalled, not unnecessarily, that the Canadian constitution of 1867 granted a special status to Quebec.
"Is Quebec not the only constitutionally bilingual province, the only one whose civil law is not merely different but protected by the constitution, the only one which is entitled to a fixed number of judges on the bench of the Supreme Court."
The agreements made since then between the governments have emphasized that special situation. For example, Quebec is the only province which collects personal income tax and applies the opting out formula. Therefore, those who reject the idea of a special status do not realize that they are thus denouncing the constitution of 1867. Only the advocates of separatism or of the associate states can logically object to the principle of a special status. All those who favour federalism must support it.
I believe that is a sound doctrine, Mr. Speaker, and he states further:
On the other hand, there are those who are tempted to suggest the more extreme forms of special status, because they believe that only a special status will allow Quebec to develop fully. In fact, those daring individuals often lack faith in the elemental strength of French Canadians. They think that the French-Canadian way of life is very fragile and, in wishing to protect it, they neglect standards of living.
I find the senator's comments very timely. That is the challenge we should give the French-Canadian youth at this time. They must compel recognition by their achieve-
The Budget-Mr. Stanbury ments in all fields, and they must not be afraid of representing but one-third of the population because the other two-thirds are not necessarily enemies; they will be members of the Canadian family where all will compete for achievement.
Mr. Speaker, I would like what my province wants to be understood in that light. Let Let there be no misunderstanding; French-Canadians do not want to dominate anyone. We merely want to live and enjoy an equal status with all other Canadians. We are even willing to learn English. Most of us are bilingual and we suggest that others, in other provinces, at least those who serve the public, should also do the same.
That is what we are asking. Let the other provinces grant us there what we grant English-speaking people in ours.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I say this. I advise the government to hurry and solve the constitutional problems. When I say that, I realize as others do that it must not be done too hurriedly either.
Here is an example. First of all, a general consensus should be arrived at in Quebec in regard to the exact details concerning the remodelling of the constitution. Agreement should be reached at least on that in Quebec.
But the people should also be aware that some good work is being done and I think the federal government is all too reticent in this respect. I think it does not stress enough the studies which are being carried out to try to brighten up the picture.
And I conclude in assuring my Englishspeaking colleagues-and I would ask them to kindly pass the word to their constituents-that Quebec will not be separatist unless it is forced into separatism through an enduring misunderstanding that would allow the continuation of a regime which has been called, and rightly so in many cases, a regime of injustice. Thank you.
