speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising in this debate I do so neither to defend the government nor to condemn it though I might be tempted to do a little of each. Sometimes those who are backbenchers of the government party envy the position of independent members such as the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain), who has just spoken, or of members of the opposition who do not have for the present, at least, the responsibilities of government. But in the light of what the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres has said it is im-
October 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Stanbury portant to recognize the importance in this house of party divisions. There is a great value, as the distinguished Speaker of the British House of Commons told us today, in the party system which has served parliaments throughout the world so well through the years. Imperfect as it is, it seems better than any other system because through it our people are provided with alternatives which are essential to the choice of government in a democracy.
Despite obligations on members of the government party to arrive at positions to be put forward and supported for the sake of stability and progress, each of us has his individual points of view which he is entitled to advance in the house. I wish to put forward today a personal point of view which has not yet been accepted by the government but I hope it will be very soon.
Before doing so I wish to comment briefly on a suggestion that, not unexpectedly, has come from the opposition.
No matter what government is in power, I suppose, the opposition will always accuse it of not giving the leadership which the country deserves. I think that such an accusation does not rest well on the shoulders of this government. Its record caused me and I presume many of my fellow freshman members on this side to seek office. I need only mention some of the ways in which this government has attacked problems which had remained neglected in this country for generations. It attacked them with courage and determination and though it lacked a majority in the house it pressed these matters forward and on many measures obtained the acceptance of all parties. The government deserves the acclaim of the country for what it has done.
I wish to mention some of the ways in which this government attacked problems of illness, ignorance and old age. In the field of illness, the health resources fund has paved the way for an orderly application of equal opportunity for and equal access to medical care as well as for a more adequate research and training program for our doctors and nurses. The fund has poured hundreds of millions of dollars already into such facilities. I hope that by July 1, 1968, medical care plans of the provinces which wish to take advantage of federal legislation will open doors to better health for Canadians of all ages and all economic levels.
In the field of education, no government has poured more money than the present one has into improving opportunities for all

time for groups inside our country to be chasing advantage or trading recriminations. The need, now, is for cool realism.
This is what I hope I can bring to bear in the specific area of public policy with which I should like to deal thiis afternoon. We have heard a great deal in recent days about housing. I do not intend to thresh over again all that old straw. To me, it is apparent that the provinces have failed-it matters little whether through inability or inaction-to cope with the problems of our growing cities, an area which undoubtedly lies within their sphere of responsibility. It is clear that our national government-and Canadians wherever they live-cannot afford to allow this failure to persist, because it is one which prejudices the future of us all, and of our country.
The Economic Council of Canada in its fourth annual review recently released says, at page 173:
It seems clear that the rising concentration of people in urban centres-and in the largest ones particularly-will continue to be closely interwoven with the projected increases in the population and labour force, and with the potential growth of output and demand in the Canadian economy.
The council observes further at page 191:
There are glaring gaps in data and information, and research into urban problems in Canada is as yet extremely limited and fragmentary.
And, later:
The regional and interurban aspects of city growth are relatively unexplored, and It appears that analytical and institutional arrangements for dealing with an emerging range of problems are scarcely developed. The task of dealing with these problems is urgent and should be a major preoccupation of provincial public policy.
I could not agree more. But is it a major preoccupation of provincial governments? Can our central government wait for provincial action or should it be galvanizing the provinces into action with a call for a concerted attack on the urban problems which will be central factors in our country's future development?
When I made my maiden speech in this house, as I had the honour of doing on the first day following the opening of this parliament, I proposed the establishment of a department of housing and urban affairs. As the representative of the most populous and fastest growing constituency in Canada I am naturally deeply concerned about the problems of urban growth. I said then that by the end of this century 90 per cent of Canadians would be urban dwellers, with probably al-

The Budget-Mr. Stanbury most half of us living in nine large cities. I called for a concentrated federal effort "to ensure for future generations a meaningful environment in the urban Canada of tomorrow".
Now, the Economic Council has told us that by 1980 over 80 per cent of our population will be urban, with 60 per cent concentrated in 29 cities or complexes of 100,000 or more residents. Further population increases, the council says, are likely to take place entirely in our cities; the pace of urbanization in Canada will continue to be one of the highest among the major industrial countries of the world. The economic benefits to be derived from urban concentration, according to the council, will thus continue to be an important factor in the longer-run rise of per capita output and income. The council goes on later to say:
The dimensions of this challenge-of the need to provide adequately for urban housing, balanced transport systems, water supply and waste disposal, parks and recreation, the control of air pollution and many other urban services, all within a framework of efficient, orderly growth and an environment of improving quality-undoubtedly call for new and imaginative public policies involving all three levels of government, including new priorities in the allocation of resources.
Reference is then made to a broad range of social questions requiring attention as a result of the continued growth of our large cities. The report states:
Many of these are closely related to the physical character of the big city and the adequacy of its services. Obvious among them are those of poverty and low income, of poor health and family breakdown, and of crime and delinquency, all of which are so frequently associated with low levels of education, bad housing, inadequate sanitation and general urban decay.
More broadly, there are in our cities growing problems of divisive social segregation and stratification, of pressures upon the individual from the hurried pace of urban living, of conflicting conformity in the comfortable suburbs, and of anonymity and lack of identification in the face of the immensity of the big city. In all these further respects, the continued rapid expansion of large centres re-emphasizes a complex of challenges if the quality of human life is to be improved, if the fruits of economic progress are to be equitably shared, and if the human resources and human potential of an urban, industrial society are to be fully developed.
e (4:00 p.m.)
The message is surely clear, Mr. Speaker. These problems are primarily provincial but they are unquestionably national as well. I ask the government whether the time has not come to recognize the central importance of these urban problems in our country, and to recognize it by establishing a department of
October 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Stanbury urban affairs and housing? I suggest that the time has come, and I hope the government will consider this step as a means of focusing our national energies and attention on the urban shape of Canada's future.
Before completing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words, not from the head but from the heart, about the unity of our country. I was encouraged by what the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) had to tell us about the views of his constituents. This summer I had the pleasure of spending a total of about four weeks in the province of Quebec, and I am pleased to say that I gained the same impression, that the people of Quebec are proud of their province, as are the people of each other province proud of their own, but above all they are Canadians.
As a member representing a Toronto riding I know there are Canadians whose language is English who cannot understand, or perhaps will not understand, the forces, the sentiments, the emotions that are present today in the province of Quebec. But I want to say to my colleagues from Quebec, and to my other colleagues in all parties whose mother language is French, I am convinced that by far the largest majority of Canadians outside Quebec would not feel as Canadian, would lose some of their pride in Canada if we were to lose that part of Canada which is the province of Quebec.
Any of us who have had any contact with Quebec, I am sure, feel it is as precious or almost as precious to us as is our own province. I hope the people of Quebec will feel the same about other parts of Canada. I hope there will be an increasing opportunity for Canadians of either official language, particularly young people, to travel across the country in order to understand better the language and the aspirations of our fellow Canadians.
We are approaching Thanksgiving weekend, Mr. Speaker. I think it would be trite to say that we have a great deal for which to be thankful. We in this country know we are faced with tremendous challenges. We know there is much that is not right, much that we can correct. But, Mr. Speaker, I think most of us in this house are convinced that nowhere in the world is there more opportunity to correct the wrongs of our society than there is in Canada, no other place in the world where the opportunity for a good life for ourselves and families is greater, and no country where the people have a greater opportunity to make a constructive contribu-

tion to the well being of their neighbours in other parts of the world. For this opportunity I am thankful, and I believe all hon. members of the house are thankful.

speechtext:

In view of the fact it appears not too likely, so far as I can determine, that there will be an opportunity to discuss this question in the house in the immediate future, I should like to make some remarks about what is happening in this field as I observed it during the recess. The remarks I intend to make will be confined largely to my observations on the Pacific coast of Canada, and in particular to the area I represent within the boundaries of which some 5,000 to 6,000 Indian people live.
Perhaps it is unfortunate that because of the juxtaposition of other events, the initiative taken by the indian affairs committee to visit the Indian people across the country was not carried through. I am unaware of any current suggestion that this project of visiting various parts of Canada to see how the Indian people are living is to be followed in the immediate future.
First of all, let me make some comment on my view of what is happening in the field of education. I am very happy to report to the house that some of the experience I had this summer in respect of this area was happy and thrilling. I had the opportunity of attending a conference organized by the extension department of the University of British Columbia with some suggestions and co-operation on the part of the Indian affairs branch. It was so designed that discussions could be held amongst the teachers who are going to teach the Indian children. I am happy to say that as a result of sitting in on those meetings for the best part of a week, I came away pleased indeed with the attitude, approach and interest shown in respect of this whole question of education of Indian people. A great deal of interest was displayed by the teachers assembled at that conference and by some of the spokesmen who addressed the conference on various topics. These included a couple of anthropologists, education experts and one or two members of the administration of the Indian affairs branch.
At that time I was also able to visit one of the old style residential schools in the Alberni valley where I make my home. It has now been completely converted into a hostel for Indian children who are not able to attend school at home because of the isolated circumstances of the particular areas in which they live. I found that the interest and attitudes of the staff there were such that one could be proud of them. It is pleasing to know that the staff includes a man and woman who have special qualifications in the field

The Budget-Mr. Barnett of consultation and guidance, and special knowledge in depth of the requirements of children living away from home, particularly those Indian children under their guidance. They have a genuine interest not only in seeing that these children obtain a proper education but also that they find themselves a proper place in life as adult citizens of the country.
In the undercurrent of the discussions that took place about the fact that all of the children living in this hostel as well as the Indian children living on local reserves in the area are now going to public schools in the community, there was a growing interest and desire that some of the culture and values of life which are cherished in the traditional Indian way on the west coast are to be taught in the curriculum of these schools. In addition, some knowledge and appreciation of these things is to be spread among those of us who come from other ethnic origins. In this field, I am happy to say that I feel we are moving in a way which will better those who are most directly concerned in these activities, at least in that particular part of the country about which I am speaking.
Let me move now to what is happening in the field of housing and community development. We have heard a great deal of discussion in the house in recent days about the whole housing question and the needs of Canadian people generally in this regard. There have been announcements made by the minister responsible for Indian affairs in respect of several programs for housing for Indian people. Some time ago there was considerable fanfare when the minister announced a program under which he said $112 million would be spent in the field of housing and community development for the Indian people. At that time a great deal of interest was aroused, and it sounded like quite a bit of money until one realized that it was a five year program and that this money was to be spread across the whole of Canada. I asked myself what difference there was in the Indian communities of my area as a result of this policy. I am very sad to report that as far as any visible evidence is concerned the results are virtually nil. Because of the expectation built up in the minds of the Indian people that we were moving in this direction, there is a growing sense of frustration and a growing sense of scepticism as to whether or not we really mean business in this area.
Let me give you an example of what I have in mind. I visited a community on
October 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Barnett Vancouver island which was slated to be visited by the committee, although this visit did not take place. Last Easter, when I visited this community and talked with members of the band council I found that they were expecting the arrival of components for four new houses to be built on their reserve. I had the opportunity of meeting one of the band councillors just before I came back to parliament and I asked him about these four houses. He informed me that they had seen no sign of them yet.
These houses were to be placed on a new town site or subdivision, as we call them in suburban terms. Let me take a minute or two to tell the house something about the kind of planning that went into this subdivision. It is beautifully laid out in sort of a crescent, at least on the map. I do not know why this particular area was chosen, but it was a mound of rock which took the shape of a regular hill. When I was there at Easter the work required to level if off had been partially done. Anyone who has had any association at all with mining will know what I mean when I say they had to drill and blast down three depths to level this off. They then pushed some sand up from the beach to fill in the holes and cracks in the rock. Out on the west coast we have a lot of rain, and the first big rain washed this sand out of the rock. A good deal of it spilled across the little grassy area around the school ruining the school playground.
Apparently they ran short of money and instead of putting the pipelines according to the plan in the rock trenches where they were supposed to be, they went straight across so that in some way or other these Indian people are going to have to get their water up to where the houses were supposed to be built.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
As I said, the new houses which were to arrive last Easter are still not there. It seems to me therefore that so far as this program is concerned the government and the people responsible for the program generally have not much to be proud of, at least judging by what is happening in my particular area of the country.
Another matter about which I would like to speak for a few minutes has to do with the question of the constitutional and legal status of the Indian people. Some of us have had the opportunity to look at the first volume of the Hawthorn-Tremblay report which deals with this question in some detail. We know this is a matter which has been discussed and

considered for quite some time. Various suggestions have been made with regard to action which may be taken in this field. I have in my hand a copy of a press release which was issued by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on September 21 of this year which quotes a statement made by the minister of that department on the same day. It reads as follows:
-work is far advanced on preparation of a new Indian Act. "Working papers which will guide the legislative drafting people in the Department of Justice have been discussed with the National Indian Advisory Council and are now being reviewed by an inter-departmental committee." the minister said. "When the final review has been completed, the act itself will be prepared and representatives of the Indian people will be consulted further."
The press release continues as follows:
The minister said that the act is being given highest priority both in the department and by the government but that there is a long standing commitment to consult the Indian people and this has inevitably slowed the process down a little.
I do not know what is meant by the phrase "slowed the process down a little" but I do know I listened to what the former superintendent general of Indian affairs had to say when he was speaking on the estimates of the branch for 1964-65 on August 14, 1964. The then minister of Indian affairs, Mr. Tremblay, was quoted as saying:
It would also be my hope that we can begin to move ahead over the next year with appropriate amendments to the Indian Act.
We are now in the year 1967. The minister's reference at that time to "next year" meant 1965. Now, the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) says that working papers are in the hands of the Department of Justice. I am not at all certain just what the minister meant when he said the act would be given a high priority. All I do know is that these matters have been dragging on far too long and that in the meantime the hopes of many Indian people for a better way of life are being frustrated as a result of the constriction imposed upon them by the present Indian Act which is in many respects outmoded.
Then again, speaking on his estimates in 1964, the minister said:
Again, we are seeking to bring about the further extension to Indians of services normally available to other citizens. This will involve continuing consultation not only with the provinces and with other federal departments but with the Indians themselves-
He then continued in some detail about the efforts that were being made at that time to
October 6, 1967

work out new arrangements through a federal-provincial ministerial conference. It is true that some steps have been taken since that time. However, it is also true that quite recently one of the ministers of the government of British Columbia, speaking to a delegation of Indians who trecked to Victoria to see him, told them simply and bluntly that so far as he was concerned Indian welfare was the responsibility of the federal government. He said that unless the federal government was prepared to foot the complete bill he was not at all interested in them. Here again, so far as the area I represent is concerned, very few practical results have been achieved in meeting what is the declared desire of the Indian people in the coastal part of British Columbia to have the same rights and opportunities in the field of education and welfare as are enjoyed by the rest of the people living in that area.
Now I would like to turn to the question of the so-called Indian claims commission. We have had in this house many discussions on this matter extending over a good many years. Hon. members will recall that on December 19, 1963 a bill was introduced with regard to this matter, Bill C-130. It was introduced by the then minister of citizenship and immigration, Hon. Rene Tremblay. The government did not proceed with the bill. It was supposed to be studied across the country and the Indian people were to be given an opportunity to make representations regarding their attitude toward the bill, after which it was to come back to the house. Representations were made by the Indian people, and on May 3, 1965 another bill was introduced by the then minister of citizenship and immigration, Hon. J. R. Nicholson, Bill C-123. The new bill was virtually the same as the original draft bill, despite the respresentations which were made by the Indian people. Hon. members may recall that after some debate the bill ceased to exist as a result of the dissolution of parliament for the 1965 general election.
If I may say so, there has been a good deal of criticism about the various actions of the government and its ministers, some of it about the head of the present government. It is my own personal view that the most irresponsible action the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of this country has ever taken was the calling of that rather stupid and ill-fated election of 1965. I am not at all sure that he would quarrel too much with that description of it in view of the later events that took place. It was certainly a waste of

The Budget-Mr. Barnett time and effort when we could have been proceeding with a constructive program on such matters as the claims commission bill. However, the fact remains that this legislation has not been reintroduced since the 1965 general election. A particular circumstance has been given by the minister as the reason for its postponement. He said many times in the house that he was postponing the introduction of a new claims commission bill until the Indians in the province of British Columbia have had a chance to get together to discuss what they thought should be done about what is known as the British Columbia Indian land question.
On the day the house reconvened after the summer recess the minister was asked a question on this subject. His reply will be found on page 2433 of Hansard, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the situation in respect of the Indian claims commission is the same as it was when the house rose for the summer vacation. Representations are still being made to us by the Indians of British Columbia that it not be introduced until they have been given an opportunity to discuss the British Columbia land question. I have again advised them that we cannot wait much longer and that I expect we will have to introduce the bill at least by next spring.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Then there was a supplementary question by the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas), who asked:
Can the minister advise the house whether he would consider setting up a deadline for the Indians of British Columbia to complete their representations so that the Indian claims commission could be set up?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, anything I have said to the Indians of British Columbia would make that quite possible.
I should like to suggest to the house and to the minister that the time has come when we in this house should stop pussyfooting around on this B.C. land question. I have no quarrel with the minister's suggesting to the Indians of British Columbia that they should get together and discuss or reappraise their thinking on the B.C. land question. But months and months have elapsed since they did that. The Indian people have met and held discussions. Not only that, but I can understand their difficulty in coming to a decision on the kind of statement they should make to the government and the parliament of Canada in view of the long and rather sorry history the whole question has had and the kind of treatment it has received from past governments and parliaments.
2906	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Barnett
One of the principal reasons that I wanted to intervene for a little while in the debate this afternoon was to suggest that this government and this parliament should come to the conclusion the time has come to speak out on this question that is such a burning one to the Indians of British Columbia. Since the union of British Columbia with Canada, the Indians have maintained that there is a B.C. land question. I think the government and the parliament of Canada should admit that there is a B.C. land question. If we were prepared to make such a declaration, then the Indian people of British Columbia would have much less difficulty at this time in making up their minds what it is they want to say to us about the matter.
The fact that has to be brought home to this parliament generally, I believe, is that there is a basic difference between what has happened in British Columbia in respect to the Indian peoples and what has happened in the rest of Canada. There is, indeed, a basic difference between what has taken place in British Columbia and what has transpired in relation to the rights of aboriginal title to land in any other part of the world that was occupied by and came under the jurisdiction of the English crown.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, there is a basic difference between what happened in British Columbia and what happened in the United States of America after that country became independent of the British crown. In fact, in no other part of the English speaking world or in the areas entered into by people from the British Isles was there such complete absence of recognition of any right of aboriginal title to land and all the things that derive from it as there was in the province of British Columbia.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in considering this question we in this parliament are dealing with a situation which is in many respects unique. We are dealing with a situation where the action that was taken in the past in this connection is no longer consistent with the kind of outlook that is generally acceptable to people in this day and age. I suggest it is our responsibility in this parliament to do what we can to redress the action that was taken in the past.
Across the rest of Canada, Mr. Speaker, we did at least go through the motions of entering into treaties with the Indian people regarding the surrendering of land. We arrived at certain agreements as a result of which certain areas of land were to be occupied by the Indians under a form of treaty which has
[Mr. Barnett.)
DEBATES	October 6, 1967
been regarded by many courts as binding in many respects, in a manner similar to international treaties that are entered into between nation states.
However, Mr. Speaker, with the exception of a small area on the southern part of Vancouver island comprising, I believe, 358 square miles in relation to which certain treaties were entered into between the head of the Hudson Bay Company, Sir James Douglas, and the Indian people in the 1850's, and an area of something like 104,000 square miles in the northeast corner of the province of British Columbia on the eastern side of the Rockies, where part of what is now British Columbia is included in the area covered by treaty No. 8, which was concluded with the Indian peoples in 1899, we have consistently denied any right of aboriginal title to the Indians in the rest of the province now known as British Columbia. This is what we mean today when we talk of the B.C. land question.
As far as the rest of the country is concerned, when reserves were set aside for the Indians under treaties the grant in land area was worked out at 120 acres per family. After confederation with Canada, under which it was agreed that treatment would be as favourable by the dominion as it had been by the crown colony, the British Columbia government took the position that the lands for the Indian peoples should not be more than ten acres per family. The federal government of that day did induce British Columbia to increase the acreage to 20 acres, but that is still only one sixth of the land which was allowed to Indians in the other parts of the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a challenging privilege to stand in this august chamber before such energetic and enthusiastic benchers and speak on the budget or any other topic. I must say that I suppose in a way it is almost presumptuous of a lowly backbencher to address a few words to the house on a budget which has been prepared and delivered by the respected Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) with the assistance of his officials. But what
October 6, 1967

can a lowly backbencher or anybody else say about a budget that finds reception in the ears of the minister?
I should like to take this opportunity to speak about the many problems that face my particular area and some of the problems that face Canada as a whole. Perhaps as I know a little more about the housing, education and transportation problems in the eastern part of Canada I should let others more experienced and knowledgeable direct their remarks to the budget.
It occurs to me that not all of us can be ministers of finance; neither can the 20 million people in Canada be officials in his department. Nevertheless, I am sure that the officials in the minister's department as well as the minister himself would like to hear from some of the representatives of the people, even from the lowly backbencher, on the subject of the budget.
As far as lack of knowledge is concerned, the opportunity exists for members to read reports by bodies such as the Economic Council of Canada and by other economists on the budget.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
For the minister's sake I think I can bend over backwards, and before becoming too critical perhaps I ought to look at the standards and guide lines which I might follow in this debate. I was surprised, of course, on looking back at a speech which our Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made in this chamber on April 17, 1962, when he was leader of the opposition, to find this as reported on page 3070 of Hansard. He was complaining about the economy and said:
We have deficits and we have jobless too. That is the ultimate in mismanagement by government.
That surprised me. The Prime Minister, who was then opposition leader judged the government by the jobless figures and deficits; yet the Minister of Finance last Wednesday, by his speech here, admitted that we have a deficit of large proportions. What many Canadians do not appreciate, however, is that we have still many without jobs. It is' not the numbers without jobs that disturbs this backbencher; it is the fact that since December, 1966, according to a statistical review, which is a publication of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics,-and I refer to volume 42 of that publication-the rate of unemployment, has been increasing.
The jobless have increased from over 272,000 to 334,000. In the light of the Prime Minister's statement when he was opposition 27053-1841
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan leader and the minister's speech of last Wednesday, this is a paradox. Nevertheless, it was said that the previous government had mismanaged our affairs.
Something else in the minister's speech of last Wednesday surprised me, and editorial comment was made about this also. The minister suggested that Canadians may face hard tasks; that they may have to make hard decisions and practice restraint. The hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) talked about tightening the belt. These are interesting words. As reported in the Globe and Mail of February 28, 1963, the present Prime Minister said at Moncton:
setting the Canadian economy right is going to require unpleasant decisions by the government.
What happened between 1963 and 1967? Why had not unpleasant decisions been taken before now? When the Prime Minister referred some years ago to judging the government by its deficits and jobless, and then presents us with this situation, may we not ask: "What has been done; what unpleasant decisions have been taken so far as the economy is concerned?" Frontbenchers and backbenchers on this side may criticize the government's course of action.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) is a courtly and kind man, but I do not think his speech of last Wednesday was courtly or kind to the Canadian taxpayer. He used words such as "readjustment", "moderation", managing the prosperity", and others similar to that. Yet, within a short period previous to that statement we had had two emergency debates, one on housing and the other on the falling price of wheat. That is enough to colour any phrases the minister might wish to use in his budget speech.
I suggest that the minister's speech of Wednesday was a canvas of camouflage. There was lots of paint but no pattern. He swung his whitewash brush, colouring everything, yet he tells Canadians that they may only use a toothbrush. The pattern that the minister painted on Wednesday had a lot of red in it; that colour was offset only by the blank looks of embarrassment on the faces of many objective members on the government side. I detected a note of apathy in the way the minister's remarks were greeted by his colleagues. There was no resounding applause for the minister, no bending over backwards. To be fair, to appreciate the minister's difficulties, it must be understood that this country is growing. As a country grows, so do its problems. One might ask whether our
October 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Nowlan problems have not been caused through our growth.
A quick look at our population figures shows that for the last five years our population has been growing at approximately 1.9 per cent a year. One can say that our growth has been approximately 2 per cent per year during the last five years. This population growth would certainly lead to more federal employees being hired. Yet, when one looks at the total numbers of federal employees, one finds that they have increased out of all proportion to population. During the first two years of this government's tenure the increase in federal employees was related to this country's growth. Between 1963 and 1964 the number of federal employees increased by 1.2 per cent. In 1965 the number of federal employees increased by 2 per cent; between 1965 and 1966, the percentage increase in the number of federal employees was 5.5 per cent, which is more than twice the increase in the population.
When one looks at the payroll increase since 1963 one finds that it is out of all proportion to the increase in population. In
1963	it increased by 8.8 per cent over 1962; in
1964	it increased by 5 per cent over 1963; in
1965	the increase was 7.2 per cent over the previous year. These figures have been taken from December of one year to December of the next. The figures for 1966 show the extravagant and inflationary increase of 19.4 per cent over 1965 in the payroll of federal employees. When one looks at those figures there is reason for concern. I suggest, none the less, that these difficulties are within the minister's control.
The minister's difficulties may be summarized fis problems of percentages. There is the 5J per cent bank rate, the 11 per cent sales tax, the 8J per cent N.H.A. maximum mortgage rate and the 30 per cent increase in labour contracts which the government has condoned. These four percentages I suggest have brought the government to its present dilemma.
That there is a dilemma is evident from reading the minister's speech. While there is talk of easy money on the one hand, the high interest rate on mortgages will help to keep it tight. This minister reminds one of King Canute who tried to hold back the tide. He has repealed the law of supply and demand. How easy can money be when we have the highest N.H.A. interest rate that this country has ever seen.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) said that the increased N.H.A. interest rate


would attract more private money into the housing field; yet he said that at a time when the investment portfolios of most private lending companies have already been allocated. At the same time, we heard a suggestion that the government might be interested in paying a rebate to offset the effects of the high interest rate. On the one hand we hear about increased interest rates and on the other hand ministers of the government suggest that a rebate might be paid to homeowners. Naturally, those who want to buy homes will be concerned about these remarks.
On Wednesday the minister suggested that he was slashing to the left and right to cut expenditures. I challenge the minister to show us where one red cent has been cut from any project or program of this fiscal year. Regardless of this fiscal year even, what has the minister removed by way of expenditure from next year's programs? He said that he had a sharp knife; yet I suggest that his knife will be dull when it comes to cutting. Every year the various departments prepare voluminous estimates for the next year; those estimates are always inflated and invariably reduced.

I challenge the minister to indicate where there has been one cent cut from this year's spending program. The hon. gentleman made his own definition of priorities when he spoke in the housing debate on October 2 as reported in Hansard at page 2731. He said, then:

Mr. Speaker, I shall first of all recall a rather sad event: tomorrow, one year will have elapsed since the Dorion tragedy which caused the death of many school children, in the riding of Vaudreuil-Soulanges.
During the last session, I had the opportunity to speak on many occasions and to urge the former minister of transport (Mr. Pickersgill) to take the most stringent safety measures to enable our citizens to use level crossings without endangering their life.
Therefore, it is on a rather grim note that I start my remarks, expressing hope that next year all necessary steps will be taken at all levels of administration to ensure maximum safety at level crossings.
Departing from that sad vein, I would now like to enjoy myself a little by recalling the recent convention of the Progressive Conservative party. The famous resolution passed by the political committee of the Conservative party to the effect that Canada is made up of two nations is certainly likely to raise a good laugh.
I feel that our friends opposite are not reminded enough of the resolution they passed, of the wish they expressed when they recognized the existence of two nations in Canada. I deplore the absence of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Churchill), one of the most fervent supporters of that resolution purporting the existence of two nations in our country, and I now wish to point out incidentally that the passage of such a resolution is nothing else than a concubinage with the Union Nationale party, in short, an attempt to gain the support of the Quebec premier, Mr. Daniel Johnson.
I have a feeling that this hoax of the Progressive Conservative party will be widely publicized so that the people will finally understand that it is nothing but bluff, because if this is really a two-nation country, there won't be any more federal-provincial conferences. No need for such conferences, with two nations within our border. There will be representatives of the French Canadian nation, facing their English Canadian counterparts.
If the Conservatives are sincere about applying this two-nation principle, they should

stop calling for federal-provincial conferences and just ask for meetings where representatives of both nations will discuss matters. If they do not do it, it is because they are neither sincere nor consistent.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, as I belong to a party whose philosophy is much more orthodox, being the doctrine of the Liberal party, I do not believe in this theory of the two nations. There may be on the cultural or sociological plan a nation that may be called French-Canadian, but there are certainly not two nations in Canada, because Ukrainians and Germans do not claim to belong to the English-Canadian nation, nor the people of Italian origin.
They are first of all Canadians, and if one wants them definitely to assume an extra title they may call themselves Canadians from Italian, German or Ukrainian origin. I say that there is no Canadian ideal and that the best way to create an ideal is first of all to ask our government, the government of all Canadians, to act as if it were really the government of all Canadians.
I think that I will not offend my Englishspeaking colleagues in saying that from 1867 until a certain period-I do not want to quote figures, dates or years-clearly the Canadian government acted as if it were only the government of the majority of the population. The existence of the French fact was tolerated and the group was handled gingerly for electoral purposes.
This is indeed the truth. The turn of mind which inspired Durham's report has not completely vanished.
Let me give an example of what is happening. Since 1945 hundreds of thousands of immigrants have entered this country. The Canadian government is not at all concerned by the fact that all these people, ninety five per cent of them assimilate the English culture. I have nothing against the fact itself. I am glad that these people can speak English. I tell myself that if the government is not concerned, it is because it is not worried about

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I
will admit that my remarks had certain caricatural aspects; nevertheless, it is interesting to see that some hon. members are not in the house, although their leader requested them to attend. I feel sorry about this, for if I were asked by my leader to be in the house, I would remain in the house, because, it must be said, we of the Liberal party have faith in our leader. There lies the whole difference.
Now, I pointed out, Mr. Speaker, how the problem of Canadian fellowship could be solved in two ways. I should like to indicate a third solution. Much has been said about bilingualism, a subject that sometimes must be broached gingerly especially when one speaks in the vicinity of the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan).

One thing is sure: the member for York-Humber, in whom I do not see a Liberal, is a man of frankness and courage.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I admit it: he is frank and courageous.
Unfortunately, his philosophy is obsolete. His philosophy is rather conservative. Yet he has the right to express his views and I congratulate him for doing so with so much vigour.
Now, Mr. Speaker, here is what I have to say about bilingualism. It is obvious that to hope for all Canadians to become bilingual would be utopian, as has been said time and time again. But bilingualism does not mean complete bilingualism. Incidentally, I find it unpleasant when members, such as the member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), for instance, demand that a clerk or a constable be bilingual. How can that be expected when even the members of the House of Commons are not bilingual?
What is being asked, for instance, is that all technical facilities be put at the disposal of the people so that they will have the right to express themselves in one of the official languages. That a member of the police force be bilingual, I do not have the right to insist on that; but I have the right to ask that my government see to it that when a French-

speaking Canadian deals with it, all the human and technical resources are used to allow him to be understood. That is why I want to eradicate the prejudice which often results from statements such as those made by the hon. member for Lapointe who asks for bilingual R.C.M.P. officers. I cannot ask that a constable be bilingual when a member of parliament, who might be a lawyer or a doctor, is not even bilingual. But we have the right to ask the government to take every possible means in order that one or the other of the two official languages in the country be understood.
